title: Digital marketing basics
summary: Plan honest, helpful marketing for a school event or small business: understand your audience, write clear messages, plan posts, help people find you online and measure what really works.
outcomes: Describe a target audience, their needs and one measurable goal for a campaign.
Write short, honest messages with one clear call to action.
Plan two weeks of posts for WhatsApp, social media and offline channels such as noticeboards.
Help a business get found with natural keywords, accurate titles and a correct Google Business Profile.
Build a contact list with permission and measure results without misusing anyone's data.
tools: A notebook or notes app and a phone are enough. Optional: the free WhatsApp Business app and a free design app such as Canva. You never need to pay for adverts in this course. Learners under 18 should plan for a fictional business, or run a real account only with a parent or guardian.

resources.title: Google Skillshop — Fundamentals of Digital Marketing
resources.note: Google's free, self-paced beginner course. It is long (about 40 hours), so pick modules that match this course, such as getting to know your customers, search, social media and email.

resources.title: Meta Blueprint — free online courses
resources.note: Meta's free, self-paced lessons on marketing with Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. Courses about paid adverts assume an adult account holder.

resources.title: WhatsApp Business app features
resources.note: Official overview of the business profile, catalog, quick replies, labels, and greeting and away messages.

resources.title: WhatsApp Help Center
resources.note: Official step-by-step help. Search for the feature you need, such as catalog, Status, broadcast lists or privacy settings.

resources.title: Google Business Profile Help — Get started
resources.note: Google's own guide to who can have a free Business Profile and how owners add, verify and update one.

resources.title: Google Search Central — SEO Starter Guide
resources.note: Google's plain-language guide to helping people find a website, including the things not worth worrying about.

resources.title: Nigeria Data Protection Commission
resources.note: The regulator for the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023. Useful background on handling people's personal data responsibly.

chapters.title: Audience, needs and goals
chapters.goal: Describe who a campaign is for, what they need and one specific goal you can measure.

sections.heading: What marketing really is
sections.body:
Marketing is not shouting the loudest or tricking people into buying. It is helping the right people find out about something useful, understand why it matters to them and decide to act. **Digital marketing** uses the same ideas on phones and the internet: WhatsApp, social media, websites, search engines and email.

Think of Malam Sani, who runs a provision shop in Kano. A clear sign outside his shop and a good WhatsApp Status post do the same job: they tell nearby customers what he sells, why it is worth the walk and what to do next. The tools change, but the thinking stays the same. Who is this for? What do they need? What do we want them to do?

sections.heading: Know your audience
sections.body:
Your **target audience** is the group of people you most want to reach. 'Everyone' is not an audience, because a message written for everyone usually speaks to no one. Narrow it down by asking:

- Who are they? For example, SS1 pupils, parents in your estate or traders at the market.
- Where are they, and when are they free to read messages?
- What do they already know about you?
- What kind of phone and how much data do they usually have?

It helps to write an **audience profile**: a short description of one typical, made-up person in that group. Giving them a name and a daily routine makes it easier to picture who will read your message.

sections.heading: Start with a need
sections.body:
People act when something meets a **need**: saving time, saving money, feeling safe, looking good, passing exams or having fun. A **feature** describes the product; a **benefit** explains what it does for the customer. 'We have a fridge' is a feature. 'Cold drinks ready at the school gate after sports practice' is a benefit.

Do not guess what people need. Ask five or six people from your audience a few short questions, such as 'What is the hardest part of buying school supplies?' or 'When do you usually check WhatsApp?' Listen more than you talk, and write down the words they use. Those words often make the best messages later.

sections.heading: Set one SMART goal
sections.body:
A campaign needs one clear goal so you know whether it worked. A **SMART** goal is Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. 'Make the science fair popular' is vague. 'Get 80 parents to confirm they will attend the science fair within two weeks' is SMART: it says what, how many and by when.

Write your audience, their need and your goal together on one card, as in the example below. Keep it in front of you while you plan every post.

code.source:
AUDIENCE AND GOAL CARD

Campaign:       Science Fair at a fictional secondary school
Audience:       Parents of JSS pupils, mostly working adults
Typical person: 'Mrs Bello', a trader who checks WhatsApp in the evening
Their need:     To know the date and time, and why it is worth leaving work early
Our goal:       80 parents confirm they will attend, within two weeks
How we check:   Count the YES replies sent to the school's WhatsApp number

points: Marketing means helping the right people discover something useful and act on it
Describe one main audience in detail instead of trying to reach everyone
People respond to benefits that meet their needs, not lists of features
A SMART goal says what, how many and by when
mistakes: Saying 'my audience is everyone' — choose the group most likely to need what you offer.
Guessing what people want — ask a few real people short questions first.
Setting a vague goal such as 'go viral' — set a number and a deadline you can check.
chapters.task: Choose a fictional school event (for example an inter-house sports day) or a small local business. Write an audience profile for one typical person, list two needs they have, and write one SMART goal for a two-week campaign.

quiz.q: A tailor in Ibadan wants more school-uniform orders before resumption. Which target audience makes most sense?
opts: Everyone in Nigeria with a phone
Parents of school pupils who live near the shop
Other tailors in Ibadan
Tourists visiting Ibadan for the weekend
quiz.why: Parents nearby are the people who need uniforms and can easily visit. A narrow audience makes the message more relevant.

quiz.q: Which of these is a SMART goal?
opts: Make the coding club famous
Post about the coding club sometimes
Get 40 students to register for the coding club within two weeks
Get as many likes as possible
quiz.why: It is specific and measurable and has a deadline, so you can check whether you reached it.

quiz.q: Which line focuses on a benefit for students rather than a feature?
opts: We use a five-litre fryer
Hot puff-puff ready in a minute at break, so you are never late back to class
Our shop opened in 2019
We have a new signboard
quiz.why: It explains what the customer gains: a quick snack without being late. The others only describe the business.

quiz.q: Why talk to a few people from your audience before planning a campaign?
opts: To learn their real needs and the words they use, instead of guessing
To collect their bank details for later
So you can copy what they post
Because the law requires exactly five interviews
quiz.why: Short conversations reveal real needs and everyday language, which make your messages more useful.

quiz.q: What is an audience profile?
opts: A list of real customers' phone numbers shared online
A short description of one typical person you want to reach
The business owner's CV
A logo and colour scheme
quiz.why: A made-up but realistic person helps you picture who will read your messages and what they need.

chapters.title: Clear messages and calls to action
chapters.goal: Write short, honest messages that say what is offered, why it matters and exactly what to do next.

sections.heading: One message, one idea
sections.body:
Most people read on a small screen while scrolling quickly. If the first line does not tell them why to care, they move on. Put the most useful information first and keep to **one main idea** per message.

A simple order that works for most posts is:

1. Who it is for, or what problem it solves.
2. What you are offering.
3. The key details: price, place, date and time.
4. One clear next step.

Use short sentences and everyday words. Read your message aloud: if you run out of breath or stumble, it is too long or too complicated.

sections.heading: The call to action
sections.body:
A **call to action** (often shortened to CTA) tells people exactly what to do next. 'Reply YES to reserve a copy', 'Tap the link to register' and 'Visit us at the school gate from 2pm' are all calls to action. 'Thanks for reading' is not.

Good calls to action are specific, easy and possible right now. If there is a real deadline, say so: 'Book by Thursday'. Use only one main call to action per message. When you give people three different things to do, many of them do nothing.

sections.heading: Honest and respectful messages
sections.body:
Trust is the most valuable thing a small business or school club has, and one misleading post can lose it. Avoid:

- **Fake urgency**, such as 'Only 2 left!' when you have plenty.
- Fake discounts, where the 'old price' was never real.
- Claims you cannot prove, especially health claims like 'this tea cures malaria'.
- Fake reviews, or using someone's photo or words without permission.

Respect also means being easy to read. Avoid writing everything in capital letters, use strong contrast between text and background on images, and add a short caption or description so that people who cannot see the picture still get the message.

sections.heading: Before and after
sections.body:
Compare the two posts below for a fictional stationery shop in Lagos. The first one shouts but says nothing useful. The second tells parents what is on offer, the price, when to come and exactly how to order.

Check the arithmetic too. Ten single books at ₦250 each cost ₦2,500, so the bundle of ten for ₦2,300 saves ₦200, which works out at ₦230 a book. Always check numbers before posting, because a wrong price causes arguments later.

code.source:
WEAK POST
BIG BIG SALE!!! COME AND BUY NOW!!! BEST PRICES IN THE WHOLE OF LAGOS!!!

STRONG POST
School resumes on Monday. Are your children's exercise books ready?
Mama Tolu Stores, Ojodu: 20-leaf exercise books, ₦250 each or ₦2,300 for 10.
Open 7am to 7pm, Monday to Saturday.
Reply BOOKS with how many you need, and we will pack your order for collection.

points: Put the most useful information in the first line
One message should have one main idea and one call to action
A call to action is specific: reply, tap, call or visit
Never use fake urgency, fake reviews or claims you cannot prove
mistakes: Writing in capital letters with lots of exclamation marks — it feels like shouting and is harder to read.
Ending without a clear next step — always say exactly what to do.
Adding several calls to action at once — choose the most important one.
Making health or results claims you cannot prove — describe what the product actually is and does.
chapters.task: Rewrite this weak post for a fictional snack business: 'WE SELL SNACKS!!! BUY NOW!!!'. In under 50 words, include who it is for, one benefit, the price, when you are open and one call to action. Read it aloud and cut any word that does not help.

quiz.q: Which is the clearest call to action?
opts: We are simply the best
Thanks for reading
Reply YES by Thursday to reserve your ticket
Tickets are available
quiz.why: It tells people exactly what to do and by when.

quiz.q: A zobo seller wants to write that her drink 'cures malaria'. What should she do?
opts: Keep the claim because it will sell more
Remove it, because it is not proven and could stop someone getting proper treatment
Write it in smaller letters
Add more exclamation marks
quiz.why: Unproven health claims are dishonest and can cause real harm. She should describe the drink honestly instead.

quiz.q: Audience: parents in Abuja choosing a holiday class for their children. Which message fits best?
opts: Coding is cool! Join us!
Two-week holiday coding class for ages 12 to 16 in Wuse. Small groups, laptops provided, ₦15,000. Reply CODE to book a free trial lesson.
We teach many things to many people every day
CLASSES CLASSES CLASSES
quiz.why: It gives parents what they need to decide (age, place, price) and one clear next step.

quiz.q: Why should the most useful information come first in a post?
opts: People scroll quickly and may read only the first line
Search engines delete long posts
It makes the post look longer
The end of a post is never shown
quiz.why: On small screens, the first line decides whether people stop and read the rest.

quiz.q: Which of these is fake urgency?
opts: 'Offer ends Friday' when the offer really does end on Friday
'Only 2 left!' when you have 50 in stock
Listing your real opening hours
Showing the real price
quiz.why: Pretending stock is running out pressures people with a false claim and destroys trust when they find out.

chapters.title: Content planning and social media
chapters.goal: Plan a simple content calendar and use WhatsApp Business and social media features sensibly.

sections.heading: Choose your channels
sections.body:
A **channel** is any route your message travels: a WhatsApp Status, a class group, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok, a school noticeboard, an assembly announcement or simply word of mouth. Choose the one or two channels your audience already uses and that you can keep up with. A busy Instagram page is no help if your audience is parents who mostly use WhatsApp.

Think about data too. Many people in your audience may be on small data bundles. Short text, small images and clips under a minute are kinder than long, heavy videos, and offline channels such as posters still work well for school events.

sections.heading: Plan a content calendar
sections.body:
A **content calendar** is a simple table showing what you will post, where and when. It stops you posting five times in one day and then disappearing for a week. A useful mix of post types is:

- **Inform**: the facts, such as date, price and place.
- **Help**: a tip that is useful even if people do not buy, such as how to keep fried snacks crunchy.
- **Show**: behind the scenes, such as students setting up the science fair.
- **Remind**: a short nudge as a deadline gets closer.

If every post says 'buy now', people stop paying attention. Mostly helpful posts build trust, so your selling posts are taken more seriously.

sections.heading: WhatsApp Business tools
sections.body:
The **WhatsApp Business app** is a free app made for small businesses, separate from ordinary WhatsApp. Its main tools are:

- A **business profile** with a description, address, opening hours and website.
- A **catalog** that shows products or services with photos, prices and descriptions. You can share a link to the whole catalog or to single items, and customers can add items to a cart and send it to you as an order message. You then agree payment and delivery with them.
- **Quick replies** for answers you type often, **labels** such as 'New order' or 'Paid' to organise chats, and automatic **greeting** and **away messages**.

**Status** updates (text, photos or short videos) disappear after 24 hours. Broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number, so politely ask customers to save it. WhatsApp has minimum age rules, so learners under 18 should practise with a fictional plan or help with a real account only alongside a parent or guardian.

sections.heading: Post responsibly
sections.body:
Being a good neighbour online keeps your audience on your side:

- Ask permission before posting photos of people, and follow your school's rules about pictures of pupils.
- Do not add people to groups or broadcast lists without asking, and make it easy to leave.
- Respect group rules: adverts in a class group meant for homework annoy people.
- Credit other people's images and ideas, or use your own.

The sample calendar below is for the first week of a fictional snack business in Port Harcourt.

code.source:
WEEK 1 CONTENT CALENDAR – Ama's Snacks, Port Harcourt

Day | Channel                              | Type   | Idea
Mon | WhatsApp Status                      | Inform | Photo of meat pies and chin-chin with prices and delivery times
Tue | WhatsApp Status                      | Help   | Tip: how to keep chin-chin crunchy for a week
Wed | Estate group (admin agreed)          | Inform | Price list and how to order
Thu | WhatsApp Status                      | Show   | 20-second clip of packing orders (no faces without permission)
Fri | Catalog link to customers who opted in | Remind | 'Order by 6pm for Saturday delivery'
Sat | WhatsApp Status                      | Show   | Thank-you post with a review shared with the customer's permission

points: Choose one or two channels your audience already uses and that you can keep up with
Mix helpful, informative, behind-the-scenes and reminder posts instead of only selling
WhatsApp Business offers a business profile, catalog, quick replies, labels and away messages
Status updates vanish after 24 hours, and broadcasts only reach people who saved your number
Ask before posting photos of people or adding anyone to a group or list
mistakes: Opening accounts on every app and abandoning most of them — start small and post regularly.
Adding people to groups or broadcast lists without asking — get permission first and make leaving easy.
Posting long, heavy videos when your audience has little data — use short clips, small images or text.
chapters.task: Make a one-week content calendar for your fictional event or business with at least four posts. For each post, write the day, the channel, the type (inform, help, show or remind) and a one-line idea. Check that no more than half of the posts are direct selling.

quiz.q: A caterer in Port Harcourt wants customers to browse her dishes and prices inside WhatsApp. Which WhatsApp Business feature fits best?
opts: Labels
The catalog
Away messages
Quick replies
quiz.why: The catalog shows products or services with photos, prices and descriptions, and customers can send chosen items to you as an order.

quiz.q: A regular customer says they never receive your WhatsApp broadcast messages. What is the most likely reason?
opts: They have not saved your number in their contacts
Broadcasts only work on Sundays
Their phone is too new
Broadcasts only reach groups of three people
quiz.why: Broadcast messages only reach people who have saved your number, so ask customers to save it.

quiz.q: Why mix helpful posts with selling posts in a content calendar?
opts: Selling posts are not allowed on WhatsApp
Helpful posts guarantee that you go viral
People trust and keep following accounts that give them something useful
Helpful posts never use any data
quiz.why: Useful tips and information build trust, so people pay attention when you do ask them to buy.

quiz.q: You want to post a photo of classmates at the science fair. What should you do first?
opts: Post it on Status because it disappears after 24 hours
Ask their permission and follow your school's rules on photos
Post it and delete it only if someone complains
Crop out the teacher and post it
quiz.why: People have a right to decide whether their picture is shared, and schools often have rules about photos of pupils.

quiz.q: What is a WhatsApp Status update?
opts: A permanent page listing your products
A paid advert shown to everyone in Nigeria
A private message to one customer
A text, photo or video update that disappears after 24 hours
quiz.why: Status updates are short-lived posts, which makes them useful for daily offers and reminders.

chapters.title: Search visibility done honestly
chapters.goal: Help people find accurate information through search by using natural keywords, clear titles and a correct Google Business Profile.

sections.heading: How people search
sections.body:
When people want something, many of them search for it. They type or speak a few words such as 'tailor near me', 'school uniform Ibadan' or 'birthday cake Enugu'. These everyday words are called **keywords**. Your job is to use the same words your audience uses, so that search engines and people can see your page, post or profile matches what they want.

To find good keywords:

- Ask customers what they would type to find you.
- Start typing in a search box and note the suggestions that appear.
- Look at the related searches shown at the bottom of a results page.

Then use those words naturally in titles, descriptions and product names.

sections.heading: Titles that tell the truth
sections.body:
A **title** is often the first thing someone sees in search results, in a catalog or above a video. A good title says what it is, where it is and who it is for, in plain words. It must match what the person will actually find.

Two tricks damage trust. **Keyword stuffing** means repeating search words unnaturally, such as 'cake cake cheap cake best cake'. **Clickbait** is a headline that promises something the content does not deliver. Google says it aims to show helpful, reliable content made for people, so honest titles and genuinely useful pages are the approach that lasts.

code.source:
WEAK TITLE
Best Cake Cake Cheap Cake Enugu Cake Lagos Abuja Cake

BETTER TITLE
Birthday cakes in Enugu – order 3 days ahead | Ada's Bakes

BETTER DESCRIPTION
Custom birthday cakes baked in Independence Layout, Enugu. Sizes from 6 to 10 inches. Collect from us or get delivery within Enugu.

sections.heading: Google Business Profile basics
sections.body:
A **Google Business Profile** is a free listing that can show a business on Google Search and Google Maps, with its address, phone number, opening hours, photos and reviews. It is meant for businesses that meet customers in person, either at a shop or by travelling to them; online-only businesses are not eligible. The owner needs a Google Account, adds or claims the business, and then completes Google's verification steps.

Follow the rules. Use the business's real name exactly as it appears on the signboard, with no extra keywords. Give a correct address and keep opening hours up to date. Reply politely to reviews, and never write fake reviews, pay for them or offer gifts in exchange for them. Learners under 18 should leave the account to the adult who owns the business.

sections.heading: Be consistent and helpful
sections.body:
Make sure your business name, address, phone number and hours are the same everywhere: on your signboard, WhatsApp profile, social pages and Google listing. Mismatched details confuse customers and search engines.

Also answer the questions people ask most, such as delivery areas, prices and how to order. A short 'frequently asked questions' post or page saves you time, helps people decide and gives search engines useful, accurate words to match.

points: Keywords are the everyday words your audience types or speaks into search
Accurate titles say what, where and for whom
Keyword stuffing and clickbait damage trust
A Google Business Profile is free and is for businesses that meet customers in person
Never buy, fake or reward reviews
mistakes: Adding extra keywords to the business name on Google — use the real name on your signboard.
Leaving old opening hours or a wrong phone number online — check your details every month.
Asking friends to write fake five-star reviews — ask real customers for honest feedback instead.
chapters.task: List five keywords a customer might use to find your fictional business or event. Then write a short, accurate title and a one-sentence description that uses two of those keywords naturally. Ask a friend whether the title tells them exactly what they would find.

quiz.q: A barber in Enugu wants to be found by people nearby. Which title is best?
opts: Barber barber cheap barber best barber Enugu Lagos Abuja
Haircuts for men and boys in Enugu – Uche's Barbing Salon
You won't BELIEVE what happened at our shop!
Welcome
quiz.why: It says what, where and for whom in plain words that people actually search for, without tricks.

quiz.q: What is keyword stuffing?
opts: Using one or two accurate words people search for
Writing a clear page title
Repeating search words unnaturally to try to trick search engines
Answering customers' common questions
quiz.why: Stuffing makes text hard to read and goes against search engines' guidelines, so it harms trust.

quiz.q: Which of these can usually have a Google Business Profile?
opts: A provision shop in Kano that customers visit
An online-only e-book seller that never meets customers
A made-up business for a class assignment
A WhatsApp group where friends share jokes
quiz.why: Business Profiles are for real businesses that meet customers in person, at a location or by travelling to them.

quiz.q: A friend offers to write ten five-star reviews for your family's shop. What should you do?
opts: Accept, because reviews help
Accept, but ask for only five
Decline, and ask real customers for honest reviews instead
Pay your friend so it is fair
quiz.why: Fake or paid reviews mislead customers and break Google's rules. Honest reviews from real customers build lasting trust.

quiz.q: Which is a sensible way to find keywords for a small business?
opts: Copy a competitor's whole website
Ask customers what they would type, and look at search suggestions
Use long technical words nobody searches for
Add random trending words
quiz.why: Customers' own words and search suggestions show how real people search.

chapters.title: Email and community building
chapters.goal: Build a contact list with permission and keep people engaged with useful updates.

sections.heading: Why your own list matters
sections.body:
Followers on a social app can disappear if an account is hacked or banned, or if the app simply stops showing your posts. A **contact list** of people who chose to hear from you, by email, SMS or WhatsApp broadcast, lets you reach them directly.

The key word is **chose**. This is called permission, or opt-in. In Nigeria, the **Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023** sets rules for handling people's personal data: collect only what you need, tell people why you are collecting it, keep it safe and respect their wish to stop. Learners should practise with fictional data and never collect other pupils' details without approval from the school and their parents.

sections.heading: Collect contacts the right way
sections.body:
Make signing up easy and honest:

- Use a sign-up sheet at an event, a short online form or a QR code on a poster.
- Ask for as little as possible, usually a name and one contact detail.
- Say what people will get and how often, for example 'one update a week about the science fair'.
- Explain how to stop, such as 'Reply STOP at any time'.

Never buy contact lists, copy numbers from a group to message people privately or add people to lists without asking. Messages that arrive uninvited feel like spam and damage your reputation.

sections.heading: Write a useful update
sections.body:
Whether it is an email or a WhatsApp broadcast, a good update has a clear subject or first line, a friendly greeting, one main message in short paragraphs, one call to action and a sign-off saying who you are. End by reminding people why they are receiving it and how to stop.

When you email many people at once, put their addresses in the **BCC** (blind carbon copy) field, not the To field. BCC hides everyone's address from the others, which protects their privacy.

code.source:
Subject: Science Fair this Friday – time, place and what to expect

Hello,

Thank you for signing up for Science Fair updates.

1. When: Friday, 10am to 1pm, in the main hall.
2. Cost: Entry is free for parents and pupils.
3. Highlight: JSS2 students will show a working solar oven.

Please reply YES if you plan to come, so we can arrange enough seats.

Kind regards,
The Science Club

You are receiving this because you signed up at the PTA meeting. Reply STOP at any time to stop these updates.

sections.heading: Build a community
sections.body:
A **community** is more than an audience: members talk to you and to each other. You build one by being reliable and human:

- Reply to messages promptly and politely, even when the answer is 'not yet'.
- Ask for feedback and show what you changed because of it.
- Use polls or simple questions to involve people.
- Share customer stories and photos only with permission.
- If you run a group, set simple rules, remove spam and handle complaints privately and calmly.

points: A contact list built with permission lets you reach people directly
Say what people will receive and how often, and make leaving easy
Collect only the details you need and keep them safe
Use BCC when emailing many people so their addresses stay private
A community grows when you reply, listen and let members help each other
mistakes: Putting everyone's email address in the To box — use BCC to protect privacy.
Buying or copying contact lists — only message people who agreed to hear from you.
Sending too many messages — agree a schedule, such as one update a week, and stick to it.
chapters.task: Design a sign-up sheet or form for your fictional campaign. It should ask for no more than two details, explain what people will receive and how often, and say how they can stop. Then draft a short first update with a clear subject line and one call to action.

quiz.q: You are emailing 40 parents about a school event. Where should their addresses go?
opts: In the To field
In the BCC field, so nobody sees the other addresses
In the subject line
In a public group post first
quiz.why: BCC keeps each person's email address private from everyone else on the list.

quiz.q: Which sign-up approach respects people's data?
opts: Ask for home address, date of birth and BVN
Add everyone from the school WhatsApp group without asking
Ask only for a name and phone number, and say you will send one update a week
Buy a list of numbers from a stranger
quiz.why: Collecting only what you need and explaining how it will be used respects people's privacy and the spirit of data protection law.

quiz.q: A subscriber replies STOP. What should you do?
opts: Send one more message to change their mind
Remove them from the list promptly and stop messaging them
Move them to a different list
Ignore it
quiz.why: People have the right to stop receiving messages, and respecting that keeps your reputation good.

quiz.q: Which subject line is clearest?
opts: Hi
URGENT!!! READ NOW!!!
Update
Science Fair this Friday: time, place and what to bring
quiz.why: It tells readers exactly what the message is about before they open it.

quiz.q: What best builds a community around a small business?
opts: Posting adverts in every group you can find
Deleting every complaint
Replying to messages, asking for feedback and sharing customer stories with permission
Only ever posting prices
quiz.why: Communities grow through two-way conversation, listening and respect.

chapters.title: Measuring results ethically and improving
chapters.goal: Choose measures that match your goal, read them carefully and improve your campaign without misusing anyone's data.

sections.heading: Match the measure to the goal
sections.body:
Numbers only help when they answer the question your goal asks. Common measures are:

- **Reach or views**: how many people saw something.
- **Engagement**: replies, reactions, shares and questions.
- **Clicks**: how many people tapped a link.
- **Conversions**: the action you actually wanted, such as tickets sold, sign-ups or orders.

If your goal is 50 ticket sales, the number that matters is tickets sold. Likes and views are sometimes called **vanity metrics**: they feel good but do not prove anyone acted. You can find numbers in many places: the list of people who viewed your WhatsApp Status, the insights on professional Instagram or Facebook accounts, your sign-up sheet, your sales record, or simply by asking customers 'How did you hear about us?'

sections.heading: Track and calculate
sections.body:
Keep a simple tracking table, like the one below, and fill it in at the same time each day. To compare posts fairly, turn counts into percentages. For example, if 200 people viewed a Status post, 14 replied and 6 bought:

- Reply rate = 14 ÷ 200 × 100 = 7%
- Purchase rate = 6 ÷ 200 × 100 = 3%

To learn which channel works best, use simple codes. Ask people who saw the Status post to 'Reply BLUE' and people who saw the poster to 'Reply GREEN', or ask each customer how they heard about you and tick a box.

code.source:
TRACKING TABLE – Reading club campaign (goal: 30 sign-ups in two weeks)

Day   | Post                    | Channel         | Views | Replies | Sign-ups
Day 1 | Club announcement       | WhatsApp Status | 180   | 9       | 4
Day 3 | Book recommendation tip | Class group     | 60    | 12      | 7
Day 5 | Reminder poster         | Noticeboard     | –     | –       | 3 (asked at sign-up)

Week 1 sign-ups: 4 + 7 + 3 = 14 of 30
Status sign-up rate:      4 ÷ 180 × 100 ≈ 2.2%
Class group sign-up rate: 7 ÷ 60 × 100 ≈ 11.7%
Next test: post the book tip on Status too, and compare.

sections.heading: Measure ethically
sections.body:
Measuring results must never mean spying on people. Responsible marketers:

- Collect only the data they need, keep it safe and delete it when it is no longer needed.
- Never share screenshots of private chats or customers' numbers.
- Never buy followers, likes or reviews. Fake numbers make your results meaningless and break platform rules.
- Report results honestly, including disappointing ones, and explain what they will try next.

Small numbers can mislead. If three people replied on Monday and five on Tuesday, that may be chance rather than a real pattern, so look for differences that repeat over several days.

sections.heading: Test, learn and improve
sections.body:
Improving a campaign works best as a series of small, fair tests. Change **one thing at a time**, such as the picture, the first line or the time of day, and compare the results with what came before. If you change everything at once, you will not know which change made the difference.

At the end of each week, write three short notes: what worked, what did not, and what you will test next. Over two weeks, these notes become a valuable record of what your audience actually responds to.

points: Choose a measure that matches the goal, such as orders for a sales goal
Likes and views show attention, not action
Use simple codes or a quick question to learn which channel brought each person
Change one thing at a time and compare results
Never buy followers, track people secretly or share private chats
mistakes: Celebrating views when nobody signed up — look at the action that matches your goal.
Changing the picture, the time and the wording all at once — change one thing so you know what worked.
Hiding disappointing results — report honestly and say what you will try next.
chapters.task: Create a tracking table for your campaign with columns for day, post, channel, views, replies and the action that matches your goal. Fill it in with realistic sample numbers, calculate one percentage step by step, and write one change you would test next week.

quiz.q: Goal: sell 50 tickets to a school drama night. Which measure fits best?
opts: Number of likes on the poster
Number of tickets sold
Number of colours on the flyer
Hours spent designing
quiz.why: Tickets sold directly measures the goal. Likes show attention, not action.

quiz.q: 250 people viewed your Status post and 10 of them placed an order. What percentage ordered?
How could you find out whether WhatsApp Status or the school noticeboard brought more customers?
opts: Guess, based on which post you liked most
Ask each customer 'How did you hear about us?' and record the answer
Count your followers
Read customers' private chats without asking
quiz.why: A quick, honest question gives real evidence without invading anyone's privacy.

quiz.q: Someone offers you 1,000 followers for ₦2,000. Why is this a bad idea?
opts: Fake followers do not buy anything and make your results meaningless
₦2,000 is too cheap for 1,000 followers
Followers can only be bought on Fridays
It is only a problem if someone finds out
quiz.why: Bought followers are not real customers, they break platform rules and they hide what your real audience is doing.

quiz.q: Your Tuesday post got more replies than Monday's, but you changed the picture, the time and the wording. What can you conclude?
opts: The new picture definitely caused it
Not much, because you changed too many things to know which one helped
Tuesday is always the best day to post
Wording never matters
quiz.why: A fair test changes one thing at a time, so you can tell which change made the difference.

project.title: A two-week campaign plan
project.brief: Plan a two-week digital campaign for a fictional school event (such as a science fair or inter-house sports day) or a small local business (such as a provision shop in Kano or a snack business in Port Harcourt). The plan must be realistic for a small team with one phone and a small data budget, and it must not use real people's personal data.
steps: Write an audience profile, the main need you are meeting and one SMART goal.
Choose one or two channels and explain why your audience uses them.
Make a two-week content calendar with at least eight posts that mix inform, help, show and remind posts.
Write three of the posts in full, each with one clear call to action.
Write an accurate search title and description, and list the details you would check on a Google Business Profile if the business serves customers in person.
Plan how you will collect contacts with permission, and draft one email or WhatsApp update.
Make a tracking table and decide which number will show whether you reached your goal.
checklist: The goal has a number and a deadline.
Every post has one main idea and one call to action.
There is no fake urgency, no fake review and no claim you cannot prove.
Photos of people and contact details are used only with permission.
The plan says what you will measure and what you will change if results are low.
